old_title: Ukraine war live: Musk hits out at Trump over Starlink after Zelensky 'betrayed'
new_title: Ukraine war live: Zelensky takes swipe at Trump and praises 'real leaders'

Elon Musk has blamed Donald Trump for restrictions imposed on his Starlink communications service, after Ukraine reported nationwide interruptions hampering frontline operations and defences against Russian attacks.
The SpaceX boss, formerly Trump's efficiency tsar, responded on Thursday to a post from Ukraine's foreign minister Mykhailo Fedorov saying the technology was "critical" for the country as officials started reporting limitations imposed on terminals moving at speed.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk said, referring to the military version of Starlink, developed by the Pentagon. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and POTUS."
While Musk has said the two systems are separate, in many cases they share the same underlying satellite technology and the distinction is not always clear-cut. Starshield's secure services use enhanced encryption and dedicated terminals, but rely on the vast Starlink constellation as their backbone.
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told the FT that the suspension was presented to Kyiv as a technical glitch, but dismissed the idea that failures of the system may have been caused by a fault: "It was not a technical problem, it was the will."
Watch: Piers Morgan issues direct television address to Trump after Zelensky's bombshell interview
Russia strikes Ukraine's Izmail port and cargo vessels
Russia has struck Izmail port in Ukraine's Black Sea Odesa region and has also hit two cargo vessels en route to Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on Telegram, claiming they were being used for military purposes.
Watch: Trump rates on-off pal Elon Musk's intelligence in Arizona rally
UK throws weight behind Ukraine amid strained ties with the US
Volodymyr Zelensky received an unprecedented honour guard made up of troops from the Irish Guards on his arrival at No 10.
The meeting came during a period of strained relations between Ukraine and the US after Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian diesel last week as high fuel prices in America threatened to overshadow November's mid-term elections.
The UK responded to news of the deal by pledging to "maintain pressure on Russia".
In recent days, the US president has also suggested Ukraine needs a new leader and claimed Russian leader Vladimir Putin wants a peace deal more than the government in Kyiv.
Mr Zelensky has also said use of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications system was "blocked" and that as a result "people will die", admitting that he felt betrayed by Mr Trump.
"It's a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner," he told Piers Morgan Uncensored.
Top story: US 'floats unfreezing some Russian assets' to restart Ukraine peace talks
The US has proposed that European countries unfreeze some Russian sovereign assets immobilised after Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and transfer them to a vehicle overseen by Washington in an attempt to revive peace talks, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday, citing people briefed on the matter.
European delegates rebuffed the plan, which was pitched by US special envoy Steve Witkoff and US president Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, the report said.
It comes after the US lifted sanctions on Russia in return for Moscow releasing some diesel to the US and global markets, according to Donald Trump.
US and Ukrainian officials had told the Kyiv Independent ahead of the deal that Russia had demanded sanctions relief as part of its talks around a then-anticipated energy ceasefire.
Trump announced an energy ceasefire had been agreed after making the diesel deal with Russia, but neither side confirmed it and strikes have continued.
Ukraine's Starshield functionality in motion has been restored, source says
Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet functionality while in motion has been restored, a source in Ukraine's defence ministry said on Thursday, a day after the crucial service was throttled at speeds of over 100 miles per hour.
The source said the defence ministry would continue to seek clarification on the reasons for Wednesday's disruption of the military-grade version of SpaceX's internet service, which affected drone missions across the frontline.
Romania still searching for seven missing sailors after ship catches fire
The Romanian Naval Authority said on Thursday it is still searching for seven missing sailors out of 12-crew on a ship which is ablaze in its territorial waters.
The ship is the second ship to catch fire near the Danube's Sulina canal after a Russian overnight attack on neighbouring Ukraine.
Burnham seeks to restore ties between the US and Ukraine
During Prime Minister's Questions, Andy Burnham said he was being "careful" in his language after Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia, as he said he was "laying the ground" for a reconciliation.
He added: "I will listen to President Zelensky carefully, but he won't be going away from Britain today empty-handed."
During his meeting with Volodymyr Zelensky, he confirmed that the UK would accelerate the supply of crucial air defence missiles to Ukraine amid "heavy bombardment" from Russia.
The accelerated support will see faster deliveries of British lightweight multi-role missiles to Ukraine, which have proved effective against Russian jet-powered drones.
Russia continues to pound Ukraine's power grid, as well as oil and gas facilities, after Mr Trump claimed that the two countries had agreed to an "energy ceasefire".
Announcing new funding for repairs at Chernobyl, chancellor John Healey said: "As the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Putin continues, our commitment to the Ukrainian people is unshakeable.
"We are curtailing the war chest funding Putin so desperately wants and backing the reconstruction of Ukraine that has suffered at the hands of his barbaric attacks."
Foreign secretary Ed Miliband said: "Our message to [Vladimir] Putin is clear - we stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail.
"Working with our allies, we are strengthening Ukraine's security, raising the cost of Russia's aggression and working towards a just and lasting peace."
Six Russian Su-34s destroyed in strike on Voronezh air base, claims Ukraine
The Ukrainian navy says it destroyed six Russian Su-34m aircraft in a fresh strike on Borisoglebsk air base in Russia's Voronezh region.
The Sukhoi Su-34 is a medium fighter-bomber and strike aircraft that entered service only in 2014. Each unit costs around $36m USD.
Britain to fund repairs to Chernobyl plant hit by Russian drone attack
Britain will fund critical repairs to the Chernobyl power plant hit by a Russian drone attack as Andy Burnham sought to bolster support for Ukraine amid "dark and difficult days" for the war-torn country.
The UK will provide £17m to help restore its protective shelter and ventilation, which were damaged by an attack last year, amid concerns that corrosion could create longer-term environmental and safety risks.
Chancellor John Healey said the government's commitment to the Ukrainian people was "unshakeable", while foreign secretary Ed Miliband said Britain will "stand shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine and will do so until they prevail".
The UK's funding pledge is part of a wider international programme coordinated by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, working alongside the Ukrainian government and G7 donors.
It comes after the prime minister hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, when he told the Ukrainian president the UK was "behind you and that will not change".

Volodymyr Zelensky praised "real leaders" for backing his country in an apparent swipe at US president Donald Trump.
The Ukrainian president said reporters it was "crucial" to count on support from allies and praised "real leaders" for backing Kyiv. "I am thankful the EU stands with us," he said.
Zelensky's comments came after Trump said Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries was a "disgrace" that would keep global energy prices elevated.
"I'm not a big fan of Zelensky," he told Newsmax. "I think they actually both would like to see it end, but I think I find Zelensky to be more difficult to deal with than Putin."
Kyiv's forces struck Russian oil refineries on Thursday, defying Trump and his "energy ceasefire".
After Russian president Vladimir Putin vowed to retaliate, Zelensky said Ukraine needed to prepare for the winter in terms of energy and air defence as Moscow had shown no sign it was ready to end the war.
Following Trump's surprise announcement on Sunday that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to halt attacks on energy infrastructure, Kyiv suspended strikes on Russian refineries. But in the days that followed, Russia was accused of launching missile and drone strikes on energy targets such as power stations.
EU leaders push back on a major budget proposal, putting a deal by end of the year in doubt
European Union leaders voiced strong opposition to a new proposal for the bloc's long-term budget, raising serious doubt about whether the key spending package will be agreed by the end of the year.
"This is far too big, far too expensive," Swedish prime minister Ulf Kristersson told reporters at an EU summit focused, in part, on trying to narrow down agreement on the seven-year budget, known as the multiannual financial framework.
"It would increase the Swedish net contribution (by) almost 60 per cent. That is simply totally unacceptable," Kristersson said. Sweden is one of about 10 net contributing countries paying more into the EU budget than they get back in allocations.
More here.
Ukrainian drones strike Russian data centre in overnight attack
Ukrainian drones have reportedly struck warehouses and a Yandex data center in Russia, according to Kyiv Independent.
Kyiv struck multiple targets across Russia's Moscow, Rostov, and Vladimir regions in an overnight attack.
The attack comes as president Volodymyr Zelensky declared that "we're done" supporting Donald Trump's energy ceasefire and resumed strikes on Russia.
How Ukrainian strikes on data centres are upending daily life in Russia
After battering Russia's version of Amazon, Ukraine has set its sights on data centres - dealing an unlikely blow to Moscow's dating scene.
A barrage of attacks on data centres and telecommunications infrastructure has wreaked havoc on Russian daily life, including three strikes in the past week on buildings owned by Yandex - the Russian equivalent of Google.
Yandex said its infrastructure had been damaged, causing the complete shutdown of its data centre in the Vladimir region on Sunday. On Wednesday, Kyiv's drones struck a data centre owned by Sberbank, the country's largest bank.
More here.
How the relationship between Trump and Zelensky soured
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have deteriorated in recent days following a meeting in Miami on 9 October that convened representatives from both countries as well as Europe and the World Bank.
President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, the US administration's Middle East envoy, struck a tough tone with Ukraine in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter.
They told Ukrainian officials that the US was frustrated with Kyiv's continued strikes on Russian refineries despite repeated requests from Washington to stop.
The US delegation also explained Washington's decision to strike a diesel deal with Russia, saying the White House hoped it would soften Moscow's stance on peace talks.
That deal, under which Russia will supply more than 2.25 million barrels of diesel to US and global markets, has triggered a backlash from some US lawmakers, who say it will give Moscow cash to pursue its war without forcing president Vladimir Putin to make concessions to end the conflict.
In the days that followed, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump criticised each other, with Zelensky calling the US decision on the Russian diesel deal "weak".
Trump in turn called for elections in Ukraine and Zelensky's ouster.
AfD leader threatens to pull German funding for Ukraine
The head of Germany's far-right party said that Berlin should end its support for Ukraine as the country is too small to defend itself against the invading Russian forces.
Alice Weidel, co-leader of the Alternative for Germany party (AfD), told The Economist that continuing the war is "not in our interest" and that it would be "wrong" to continue financing what she called "an already lost war".
"Ukraine is too small. Ukraine cannot win against Russia. It is impossible," she said, adding: "We are about to spend over 100 billion. No other country has spent that much, and we are highly indebted. I have the interest of my country first; it's Germany first and this war is not in our interest."
More here.
Trump says Zelensky 'not a good guy' and calls for Ukraine elections
US president Donald Trump has criticised Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky, calling him "not a good guy".
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax."
He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. I'm not a big fan of Zelensky. They've destroyed that country," Trump added.
Trump reiterated his call for an election in Ukraine. Trump criticized Zelenskyy over strikes on Russian oil refineries, arguing that the attacks were driving up energy prices.
"I think that's a disgrace. There's plenty of other targets," Trump said. "When you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world," he added.
Ukraine testing new 'evacuation drone' that rescues wounded soldiers
Six propellers whir to life, lifting a huge drone above a field in Ukraine. A weighted stretcher secured to its frame simulates a wounded soldier in body armour.
Far from the front line, the demonstration offers a glimpse of a far more dangerous mission: flying into a battlefield where enemy drones and artillery can leave wounded troops stranded for weeks or months, then carrying them to safety without an evacuation crew.
The aerial medical evacuation drone was developed over the past year by Ukrainian defence technology company SkyFall.
More here.
Trump says Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is 'disgrace'
Ukraine's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries is a 'disgrace' that keeps global energy prices elevated, US president Donald Trump has said.
Ukraine struck a Russian oil refinery after president Volodymyr Zelensky declared that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire covering energy sites that Trump had announced, and criticised his willingness to strike deals with Moscow.
"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump told Newsmax after Ukraine hit a Rosneft refinery southeast of Moscow which helps to supply the Russian capital.
"There are a lot of targets you can hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he's not doing a good service for the world."
Trump says he is talking to Russia and China about denuclearization
US president Donald Trump said Washington was holding talks with Moscow and Beijing aimed at denuclearizing the countries with the biggest stockpiles of nuclear weapons.
Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The US outpaces Russia on its number of deployed warheads.
During an interview with Newsmax, Trump said he expects China to "catch up" with the US within the next five years.
"The whole thing is a shame, because I'd love to denuclearize if possible, but we're actually talking to Russia about that, and we're talking to China about that denuclearization," Trump told the outlet.
Order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside White House - report
The order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, two US officials and a Western official told Reuters.
The officials said leaders at the defence department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
The officials did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order. The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
Ukrainian officials said this week that military-grade Starlink receptors stopped working in Ukraine when mounted on fast-moving objects, interfering with the performance of Ukrainian drones that rely on them for onboard guidance systems over Ukrainian territory.
